name: Mingles
summary: Seoul's only three-Michelin-star restaurant: Chef Kang Min-goo's modern Korean tasting menu built on jang (fermented sauces).
description: Mingles is the sole three-star restaurant in the MICHELIN Guide Seoul 2026 and was named Korea's best restaurant on Asia's 50 Best in 2024. Chef Kang Min-goo cooks modern Korean food anchored in doenjang, ganjang and gochujang, served in a calm, wood-toned Cheongdam dining room. Courses change with the seasons, with Korean-liquor and wine pairings. It is the ultimate celebration meal of the trip — book as early as possible.
tips: Lunch (₩320,000) is the less expensive way in; dinner is ₩420,000 per person (Naver menu, 2026).
Book on CatchTable as soon as slots open; ask for a table for five well in advance.
Closed 24–27 Sep per the owner's Naver holiday schedule.
Valet parking; Apgujeong Rodeo Station Exit 3, ~8 minutes.

reviews.text: Travellers describe a quietly thoughtful experience using traditional Korean ingredients and flavours — an amazing culinary experience.
Dinner at ₩420,000 feels steep, but the service and finish of every dish are clearly three-star level (Aug 2026).
A meal worthy of its three stars — Korean tradition reinterpreted with a modern sensibility (Jul 2026).

price.note: Lunch ₩320,000; dinner ₩420,000 per person, drinks extra (Naver menu, 2026)

hours.note: Break 15:00–18:00. Sunday closed; Monday is listed differently on Naver (open 28 Sep) and Kakao (closed) — confirm when booking.

chuseok.note: Closed 24–27 Sep per the restaurant's Naver Place holiday schedule. Reopens by 29 Sep; Mon 28 Sep unclear — confirm when booking.

name: Onjium
summary: Royal-court and noble-household recipes reimagined, facing Gyeongbokgung's stone wall — Michelin one star.
description: Onjium is the restaurant of a research institute devoted to Korean heritage food, clothing and architecture. Its team studies Joseon-era court and aristocratic recipe books and turns them into precise seasonal tasting menus. The fourth-floor room is calm and minimal, looking across to the western wall of Gyeongbokgung Palace. It holds one Michelin star in 2026 and is one of Seoul's hardest reservations.
tips: Lunch ₩200,000 vs dinner ₩300,000; Korean-liquor pairing is cheaper than wine (Naver menu, 2026).
Book the moment slots open; tables for five are rare, so ask early.
Closed Sundays, Mondays and 24–26 Sep (Chuseok).
Pair with a Gyeongbokgung visit; Gyeongbokgung Station is about 8 minutes away.

reviews.text: Royal court cuisine that leans simple and clean — a great introduction to food 'sophisticated enough for royalty'.
Dinner course (₩300,000) of 12 dishes on 30 Jul 2026; the reviewer felt it speaks a Korean culinary language only this place can show the world.

price.note: Lunch ₩200,000; dinner ₩300,000; pairings ₩80,000–180,000 (Naver menu, 2026)

chuseok.note: Closed 24–26 Sep for Chuseok per Naver Place notice; also closed Sun 27 and Mon 28 (regular closures).

name: Jungsik
summary: The restaurant that launched 'New Korean' — playful two-Michelin-star tasting menus in a sleek Cheongdam house.
description: Jungsik opened in 2009 and became the reference for modern Korean fine dining, later spawning Jungsik in New York. Dishes are witty and visual — the signature gimbap bites and dolhareubang dessert are Instagram staples — with staff explaining each course in fluent English. The multi-level Cheongdam building has private rooms for 2–10 guests, which suits a family of five. It holds two Michelin stars in 2026.
tips: Lunch ₩230,000 vs dinner ₩330,000 (Naver menu, 2026).
Request a private room (2–10 guests) for a family of five.
Open daily 12:00–22:00 with a 15:00–17:30 break; no Chuseok notice found — confirm when booking.
Valet parking available; Apgujeong Rodeo Station ~8 minutes.

reviews.text: Staff present each dish in perfect English; every course is creative, uses the finest ingredients and looks as good as it tastes.
A family of four did the dinner course with a five-glass pairing on 1 Aug 2026 and enjoyed it as a special occasion.
A good 'first fine dining' — polished flow, harmonious ingredients and refined service (2026).

price.note: Lunch ₩230,000; dinner ₩330,000 per person (Naver menu, 2026)

name: La Yeon (The Shilla Seoul)
summary: Two-Michelin-star Korean haute cuisine on the Shilla's 23rd floor, with Namsan views and private rooms for families.
description: La Yeon is The Shilla Seoul's Korean restaurant, holding two Michelin stars in 2026. Courses revisit classics such as sinseollo (royal hot pot) and gujeolpan in a hushed, elegant room with sweeping views over Namsan and the city. A vegetarian course is available, and private rooms seat 6–10 — ideal for parents who prefer quiet and formality. Service is classic five-star hotel.
tips: Lunch course ₩250,000 vs Shilla dinner course ₩380,000 (Naver menu, 2026).
Private rooms seat 6–10 — book one for the family.
Hotel restaurant with daily hours; no specific Chuseok notice found, so confirm when booking.
Valet parking; Dongguk University Station Exit 5 plus hotel shuttle/walk.

reviews.text: Opinions are split: some diners rate it on a par with the best Michelin restaurants with flawless service and views; others found dishes bland for the price.
Refined Korean dishes by chefs Kim Seong-il and Cha Do-young — familiar yet elevated (Sept 2026).
A non-vegetarian tried the vegetarian course and found it just as impressive (May 2026).

name: Bicena
summary: Michelin-star Korean tasting menus on the 81st floor of Lotte World Tower — the most dramatic dining view in Seoul.
description: Bicena sits on the 81st floor of Lotte World Tower, Korea's tallest building, with floor-to-ceiling views over the Han River and Jamsil. The cooking is refined Korean with a Gyeongsang-do accent: house-dry-aged hanwoo sirloin, pork belly and seasonal banchan served on beautiful ceramics. It holds one Michelin star in 2026. Combine it with Seoul Sky or the Lotte World Mall below for a futuristic Jamsil day.
tips: Lunch Sancheon course ₩170,000 (weekday/weekend/holiday) vs dinner ₩280,000 (Naver menu, 2026).
Book a window table at sunset for day-to-night views.
Owner-set Chuseok hours on Naver: open 12:30–22:00 on 24–26 Sep.
Jamsil Station (Lines 2/8) connects underground to Lotte World Mall.

reviews.text: Fine dining with small portions but glorious, super-refined dishes and spectacular city views.
'I didn't know a plate of Korean food could be this beautiful' — a lunch that made the reviewer truly happy (Jun 2026).
Naver visitors rank 'great view' almost as often as 'delicious food' and 'special-occasion place'.

price.note: Lunch ₩170,000; dinner ₩280,000 per person (Naver menu, 2026)

chuseok.note: Open 12:30–22:00 on 24, 25 and 26 Sep per owner-set Chuseok hours on Naver Place.

location.address: 81F, Lotte World Tower, 300 Olympic-ro, Songpa-gu, Seoul

name: Eatanic Garden (Josun Palace)
summary: Michelin-star 'urban garden' tasting menu 36 floors above Gangnam — the closest star to home, with sweeping city views.
description: Eatanic Garden occupies the 36th floor of Josun Palace in Yeoksam, a few Line 2 stops from home. Chef Son Jong-won builds each seasonal course around one Korean ingredient, introduced with an illustrated card, and plates it with a strong visual identity. Window tables look over Gangnam's towers, especially dramatic after dark. It holds one Michelin star in 2026 and appeared on Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2024 (#62, extended list).
tips: Lunch ₩250,000 vs dinner ₩370,000 (Naver menu, 2026).
Closed Mondays and Tuesdays — 28–29 Sep won't work.
No specific Chuseok notice found; Kakao shows normal hours 24–27 Sep — confirm when booking.
Yeoksam Station Exit 8, ~7 minutes; ≈15 minutes from home by taxi.

reviews.text: Reviewers describe each dish as a symphony of flavours, praising the plating, seasonal ingredients and impeccable service.
Delicious food, a wide wine list, kind service and a great view — 'go and be happy' (Sept 2026).
A food blogger praised contemporary Korean cooking with a gorgeous view over Seoul from the Josun Palace dining room.

price.note: Lunch ₩250,000; dinner ₩370,000 per person (Naver menu, 2026)

name: Soseoul Hannam
summary: Michelin-star modern Seoul cuisine in a sleek Hannam basement — kelp chips, aged kimchi, chargrilled webfoot octopus.
description: Soseoul Hannam expresses 'today's Seoul' through ingredients locals know well: kelp chips, rich doenjang stew, raw fish with gomchwi greens, aged kimchi and charcoal-grilled webfoot octopus. The room is very modern and minimal, and staff explain each course in detail. It holds one Michelin star in 2026. A good choice for a design-loving family who want contemporary Korean without Cheongdam formality.
tips: Reserve well ahead; ask for a table for five when booking.
Hours and Chuseok opening could not be verified online — confirm by phone (+82-2-797-5995).
Located in Hannam-dong; taxi is simplest from home (≈20 minutes).

reviews.text: Very modern decor, impeccable service and polite, efficient staff who explain every dish in detail.
Not everyone agrees: one recent reviewer felt the experience was poor value and strongly warned others off.

price.note: Tasting menus; MICHELIN Guide price range 'Spare no expense' — current prices not published online, confirm when booking

hours.note: Opening hours not verified for 2026 — check when booking.

name: Kwonsooksoo
summary: Two-Michelin-star Korean tasting menus with a famous kimchi cart and private rooms — refined, calm, Cheongdam.
description: Chef Kwon Woo-joong's Kwonsooksoo takes its name from the old term for a family's private cook, and the food leans on traditional preserves, jang and heirloom ingredients. A trolley of house kimchi and jangajji is wheeled to the table mid-meal. Private rooms make it a strong option for a family celebration — a Naver reviewer booked one for a family Christmas Eve dinner. It holds two Michelin stars in 2026.
tips: Lunch ₩240,000 vs dinner ₩380,000 (Naver menu, 2026).
Book a private room for five; valet parking available.
Closed Sundays, Mondays and 25–26 Sep; open 24 Sep.
Apgujeong Rodeo Station Exit 3, ~10 minutes.

reviews.text: Modern Korean fine dining with a cart of eight kimchis; one reviewer called it by far the most incredible restaurant they visited in Seoul.
Booked a private room for a family Christmas Eve dinner — comfortable and private for the whole family (Dec 2025).
The lunch course was very satisfying; care was evident in every dish (Jul 2026).

price.note: Lunch ₩240,000; dinner ₩380,000 per person (Naver menu, 2026)

name: Balwoo Gongyang
summary: Buddhist temple-food courses opposite Jogyesa — calm, vegan, seasonal and gentle on the stomach.
description: Run by the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism, Balwoo Gongyang serves temple cuisine: no meat, fish, garlic or onion, relying instead on mountain greens, fermented jang and seasonal produce. Courses range from a weekday-lunch Seon-sik set to the pre-booked Hui-sik feast. The fifth-floor rooms overlook Jogyesa Temple and feel serene after Insadong's crowds. It held a Michelin star for several years but is not listed among the 2026 starred restaurants.
tips: Weekday lunch Seon-sik is the best value; Hui-sik (₩120,000) needs advance booking.
Naver reviewers bring parents for a healthy, mild meal.
Closed Sundays and 24–26 Sep (Chuseok).
Anguk Station Exit 6, ~5 minutes; combine with Insadong and Jogyesa.

reviews.text: Many praise the gourmet vegan temple food, presentation and service; a minority found some dishes bland or cold.
Brought a father visiting from Busan for his health; mild, clean dishes suited him perfectly (Aug 2026).
Every dish excellent — it takes things away rather than adding, to let each ingredient speak (Aug 2026).

price.note: Seon-sik weekday lunch ₩36,000; Won-sik ₩50,000; Maeum-sik ₩70,000; Hui-sik ₩120,000 (Naver menu, 2026)

chuseok.note: Closed 24–26 Sep per Naver Place Chuseok notice, and Sun 27 (regular closure).

name: Born & Bred
summary: Hanwoo beef omakase from a Majang-dong butcher family: four floors, staff-grilled cuts, private rooms
description: Born & Bred grew out of a hanwoo wholesaler that has traded beef in the Majang-dong meat market since 1978, and it claims Korea's first hanwoo omakase. The new building has a different concept on each floor. The basement Speakeasy serves the full omakase at one 19:00 seating, the 2F hall has à la carte cuts and a casual tasting menu, and 3F has private rooms serving a shorter 13–14-course menu. Staff grill every cut at the table and explain it. The room is polished, with marble counters, copper grills and a butcher case by the door. It is listed in the 2026 MICHELIN Guide and appeared on Asia's 50 Best Restaurants' extended 51–100 list in 2024.
highlights: 2F casual tasting menu with yukhoe (beef tartare) and a mixed beef platter
Brisket hot-pot rice with soybean-paste soup
tips: For five people, book a 3F private room on CatchTable. Lunch there costs ₩230,000 per person, less than dinner (₩280,000).
The 2F hall is the cheaper way in: a 200 g hanwoo platter is ₩100,000 and staff still grill it for you.
Majang Station (Line 5) Exit 3 is a 4-minute walk. You pass the huge Majang meat market on the way.
Closed Tuesdays. The break is 15:00–18:00 and last order is 21:15. Corkage is free for one bottle per person.

reviews.text: Amazing Hanwoo beef. They will assist to cook the meat, explain each cut.
Best meal of our holiday...every bite was delicious and our sweet and attentive server made sure the meat was prepared perfectly.
reviews.author: Paloma

reviews.text: Naver visitors most often praise the flavour and quality of the beef and the friendly service, and call it a place for special occasions with an impressive interior.
Inspectors highlight top-grade hanwoo from Majang-dong, with a different concept on each floor, from burgers and steaks to tasting and chef's-choice menus.

price.note: 2F: hanwoo platter 200 g ₩100,000 or 300 g ₩130,000; casual tasting ₩165,000. 3F private room: lunch ₩230,000, dinner ₩280,000. B1 omakase ₩380,000 (Naver menu, 2026).

hours.note: The regular day off is Tuesday, and the break runs 15:00–18:00. The B1 omakase has one dinner seating at 19:00. Lunch has one seating, and dinner has two on 2F and 3F.

chuseok.note: The restaurant's Naver Place hours show it closed Thu 24 – Sun 27 Sep for Chuseok. It reopens Mon 28 Sep. The same listing shows special hours on Tue 29 Sep, normally the day off, so confirm when you book.

name: Samwon Garden
summary: Apgujeong's big galbi house since 1976: marinated short ribs grilled by staff, beside a landscaped garden
description: Samwon Garden has served marinated galbi (short ribs) in Apgujeong since 1976, and it reopened in 2022 after a full rebuild. The new building has high ceilings and glass walls onto a landscaped garden, which makes the large hall bright and calm even when it is full. Staff grill the beef at the table, from the signature soy-marinated galbi to hanwoo sirloin and special cuts. There is also a long list of dishes for people who don't want meat, such as naengmyeon, galbi-tang and ganjang-gejang (soy-marinated crab). The MICHELIN Guide lists it as a Selected restaurant for 2026, recommended for groups.
highlights: Weekday lunch set with hanwoo bulgogi (₩55,000)
Naengmyeon to finish (a ₩11,000 taster portion is on the menu)
tips: The weekday-only lunch set costs ₩55,000 per person (minimum two people). You choose hanwoo bulgogi, soy crab or barley-dried croaker, with naengmyeon or doenjang stew, which makes it the good-value way in.
Private rooms seat groups. Book one for five on CatchTable, especially for dinner and weekends.
Order a small taster naengmyeon (맛보기 냉면) after the galbi, as Korean regulars do. Parking is easy, and on Naver it is often praised as roomy and clean.
Apgujeong Station (Line 3) Exit 3 is about an 8-minute walk. The break is 14:30–17:30 on weekdays and 14:30–17:00 at weekends.

reviews.text: Korean diners most often mention the tasty food, the spacious hall, the handsome interior, fresh ingredients, and that it suits group gatherings.
Inspectors note skilled staff grilling of prime Korean beef, and a landscaped garden seen through high glass walls that makes the room feel spacious.

name: Byeokje Galbi (Bangi flagship)
summary: Seoul's blue-chip hanwoo galbi house: top-grade marbled short rib and ribeye, plus classic Pyongyang naengmyeon
description: Byeokje Galbi has served hanwoo short ribs since 1986, and Korean families book the Bangi-dong flagship near Olympic Park for big celebrations. It buys only top-grade cattle (BMS No. 9) at auction, and in-house butchers cut the beef. The signatures are the 'Seolhwa' diamond-cut saeng-galbi (short rib) and kkot-deungsim (ribeye), grilled for you over charcoal. There is also a serious Pyongyang-style naengmyeon and hanwoo soups for lighter eaters. Staff are formal, the dining rooms are hushed, and upstairs rooms suit a family of five. VisitKorea notes its recognition in the MICHELIN Guide Seoul 2023.
highlights: Seolhwa saeng-galbi (diamond-cut hanwoo short rib), 200 g ₩160,000
Seolhwa galbi-tang or oxtail soup lunch sets
tips: Lunch (11:30–15:00) is the smart way in. A 120 g sirloin set costs ₩69,000 and a mixed-cut set ₩59,000 (minimum two people). Soup and naengmyeon trays are ₩35,000–45,000.
Book on CatchTable and ask for a 2F private room for five.
Bangi Station (Line 5) Exit 4 is a 3-minute walk. Pair it with a walk in Olympic Park or a trip to Lotte World Tower.
On TripAdvisor, a few foreign diners complain of rushed service at peak dinner times. Go at a quieter lunch or early-evening slot.

name: Mongtan
summary: Straw-fire-seared beef short ribs grilled by staff in a converted old house by Samgakji — Seoul's most-queued BBQ.
description: Mongtan made its name with u-dae-galbi: thick bone-in beef short ribs seared over burning rice straw (jjipbul) downstairs, then finished at your table by staff. The building is a renovated older house near the War Memorial, with a bustling open grill room on the ground floor. Expect a smoky, fragrant, lively room rather than a quiet one. Queues are legendary, but the payoff is some of the most talked-about beef in the city.
highlights: Yangpa bokkeumbap (onion fried rice) to finish
tips: Kakao lists a CatchTable page; walk-in waits of about an hour are common on weekends (per a Sept 2026 Naver blog). Arrive before the 12:00 opening or go mid-afternoon on a weekday.
Short rib is ordered by 280 g portion with a two-serving minimum; staff do all the grilling.
Group tables seat 5–6 (Naver seating info) — say you are five when you register.
No on-site parking; Samgakji Station Exit 8 is a 1–3 minute walk.

reviews.text: Reviewers rave about tender, high-quality beef and the distinctive flavour from the straw-fire searing; several warn of the queue and that the toilet is outside the dining room.
A Naver blogger (Sept 2026) waited an hour on a weekend; loved the ribs but noted three light eaters still spent over ₩200,000 — a treat, not a bargain.
Naver visitors most often tag it 'the food is delicious' and 'the meat quality is good', and praise staff who grill everything for you.

price.note: U-dae-galbi ₩35,000 per 280 g serving (2-serving minimum); hangjeong-sal ₩18,000; naengmyeon ₩8,000 (Naver menu, 2026)

name: Daedo Sikdang (Wangsimni main)
summary: Hanwoo sirloin on cast-iron since 1964 — Seoul's classic beef house, finished with legendary kkakdugi fried rice.
description: Daedo Sikdang has been grilling thick-cut hanwoo sirloin on heavy iron plates in Wangsimni since 1964, and the main branch is still where Seoulites take their parents for a beef night. The menu is short: sirloin, a few special cuts, and kkakdugi (radish kimchi) fried rice made in the beef fat at the end. The main store has been refreshed and expanded into annex buildings, and Naver reviewers mention good ventilation and a spacious room. Prices are high but well below Cheongdam steak houses for comparable hanwoo.
tips: Private rooms seat 4–12 (Naver seating info) — request one for a family of five.
Always leave room for the kkakdugi fried rice (₩6,000); regulars consider it the point of the meal.
Valet and paid parking available; by subway use Sangwangsimni Exit 2 (≈6 min) or Wangsimni.
Recent reviewers note grilling can be self-service at busy times — ask staff to help.

reviews.text: Travellers compare it favourably with famous steakhouses: top-quality cuts and very high-quality beef at prices far below New York steak houses.
A family dinner review (Sept 2026): walked straight in on a Friday night, sirloin then kkakdugi fried rice; the big room is well ventilated and comfortable.
Returning diners say the renovated main store and new annex buildings feel clean and pleasant, and the meat is as good as ever.

name: Hanilkwan Apgujeong
summary: Seoul's grande dame of Korean cooking since 1939 — bulgogi, galbitang and Seoul naengmyeon in a calm Apgujeong house.
description: Hanilkwan opened in Jongno in 1939 and is one of Seoul's oldest restaurant names; its Apgujeong flagship is where three-generation families gather for bulgogi, galbitang and Seoul-style cold noodles. The menu is broad and gentle rather than fiery, which suits parents and first-timers alike. Dishes are neat and mild, service is polished, and valet parking makes it an easy family dinner stop. It is about three stops from home on Line 3.
tips: Lunch sets (bulgogi ₩39,000 / galbi ₩49,000) are the easiest way to try the classics.
Naver reviewers call it ideal for dining with parents — mild, clean flavours and quiet rooms.
Valet parking available; Apgujeong Station Exit 2, about 5 minutes on foot.
Galbitang (₩20,000) plus a shared bindaetteok makes a lighter, cheaper meal.

name: Wangbijib Myeongdong Main
summary: Staff-grilled marinated pork and hanwoo in the middle of Myeongdong — the easy, visitor-friendly BBQ after shopping.
description: Wangbijib is a Myeongdong institution for galbi and marinated pork, set on a second floor a few minutes from Myeongdong Station. Staff grill for you, the side dishes are neat, and room-like booths make it calmer than the street outside. It is used to foreign guests, which makes ordering easy, and lunch sets arrive already cooked. It is not a hidden gem, but it is a reliable, comfortable BBQ in the city's busiest shopping district.
tips: At lunch the set meals come pre-grilled — no smoke on your clothes before an afternoon of shopping (Naver review).
Booth-style tables give a quieter meal; good for five.

Sweet charcoal-scented pork galbi, good value right in central Myeongdong — suits all ages and foreign visitors.

name: Geumdwaeji Sikdang (Gold Pig)
summary: Michelin Bib pork BBQ in Yaksu: thick YBD pork belly grilled by staff, wrapped in grilled basil — worth the famous queue.
description: Gold Pig is often named among Seoul's top three pork houses and holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand. It uses YBD crossbreed pork — thick 'bon-samgyeop' belly and snowflake-marbled neck — grilled for you over charcoal and served with a signature grilled-basil wrap. Staff scrub the grill and extractor between parties, so the three-storey building stays cleaner than a typical pork joint. The whole-pig kimchi jjigae is a cult side order.
tips: No bookings: register on the CatchTable on-site waitlist from about 10:00; a Sept 2026 reviewer got #25 at 10:00 and was seated ~11:45.

name: Woo Lae Oak
summary: Since 1946: the benchmark Pyongyang cold noodles in hanwoo broth, plus old-school bulgogi — a Michelin Bib Seoul legend.
description: Woo Lae Oak has served Pyongyang-style naengmyeon in Euljiro since 1946, and many Seoulites still consider it the reference bowl. The broth is simmered from hanwoo shank and seasoned only with salt and soy, so it tastes clean and beefy rather than sweet. Big, bright dining halls over two floors take families easily, and bulgogi grilled at the table makes a classic pairing. It is listed as a Bib Gourmand in the MICHELIN Guide Seoul 2026.
tips: Weekend waits of 1.5–2.5 hours were reported in Aug 2026 — register at the door and explore Gwangjang Market or Cheonggyecheon while you wait.
Weekdays have a 14:00–17:00 break; arrive at 11:30 or just before 17:00.

name: Eulmildae
summary: One of Seoul's 'big four' Pyongyang naengmyeon houses — slushy-cold broth, thick buckwheat noodles and mung-bean jeon.
description: Eulmildae in Yeomni-dong is counted by Korean noodle fans among Seoul's four great Pyongyang naengmyeon houses. Its broth is served ice-slushy with a bolder flavour than Woo Lae Oak, and regulars order 'georaeng' (no ice) or 'yang manhi' (extra noodles) by code. Suyuk (boiled beef) and nokdu-jeon (mung-bean pancake) make it a proper meal. It is a busy, no-frills local institution rather than a polished dining room.
tips: Order like a regular: 'georaeng' = broth without the ice slush, 'yang manhi' = extra noodles.
Queues move fast; there is a shaded waiting area. Rainy days mean shorter lines (Naver reviewers).
Closed the whole Chuseok break — go 23 Sep or from 28 Sep.

reviews.text: Reviewers call it authentic Pyongyang-style naengmyeon with great noodle texture and finely crushed ice; locals queue even before noon.
Visited one of Seoul's four great Pyongyang naengmyeon houses and found it lived up to its reputation (Sept 2026).
Waited about 15 minutes at 12:30 on a Friday; shade and cool air at the queue made it bearable.

summary: Michelin Bib Pyongyang naengmyeon near Namsangol Hanok Village — clear, peppery broth and handmade mandu.
description: Pildong Myeonok belongs to the Uijeongbu school of Pyongyang cold noodles: a very clear, lightly peppery broth topped with chilli flakes and scallion, and firm buckwheat noodles. It sits by Chungmuro Station, a short walk from Namsangol Hanok Village. The dining room is plain and calm; the menu is naengmyeon, bibim, onmyeon, jeyuk (boiled pork) and dumplings. highlights: Bibim naengmyeon with sweet soy dressing
tips: Combine with Namsangol Hanok Village (5 minutes' walk).

Travellers describe a Pil-dong landmark for Pyongyang buckwheat noodles with a light broth and chewy noodles, plus good mandu soup.

name: Myeongdong Kyoja
summary: Seoul's most famous kalguksu since 1966: rich chicken-broth noodles, thin-skinned dumplings and fiery garlic kimchi.
description: Myeongdong Kyoja has served the same short menu — kalguksu, mandu, bibim-guksu and summer kongguksu — since 1966, and Naver shows over 40,000 visitor reviews. The noodles come in a thick chicken-and-beef broth with tiny wontons and minced meat; the garlicky kimchi is famously potent. Service is lightning-fast: you pay upfront and noodle refills are free. It is listed in the MICHELIN Guide Seoul 2026.
tips: Tell the door staff how many you are and they send you to a floor — turnover is fast even when the line looks long.
Pay first; ask for extra noodles (sari) at no charge.

name: Hadongkwan
summary: Clear brass-bowl gomtang since 1939 — Myeongdong's breakfast beef soup that closes when the pot runs dry.
description: Hadongkwan has served one dish, gomtang, since 1939: a clear, deeply savoury beef broth with brisket (and tripe if you like) over rice, served in brass bowls. You pay first, choose your size, add scallions and the Seoul-style kkakdugi, and eat quickly among office workers. It opens at 07:00, making it one of the best early breakfasts in central Seoul. It appears in the MICHELIN Guide Seoul 2026.
tips: Go for breakfast (07:00–09:00) to avoid the lunch rush and catch the freshest pot.
Pay at the counter first; ₩18,000 is meat-only, ₩25,000 adds offal ('naejang manhi' for extra).
Regulars add lots of scallion and skip pepper at first to taste the broth.
Closed Sundays; closes at 16:00 or earlier if sold out.

reviews.text: Came at 08:00 on a weekday for a hangover breakfast — quiet, and the basic gomtang was clean and comforting (Aug 2026).

name: Tosokchon Samgyetang
summary: Seoul's famous ginseng-chicken soup in a rambling hanok near Gyeongbokgung — nutty, thick broth and fast queues.
description: Tosokchon is the samgyetang house every guidebook mentions, and it is still packed with Koreans as well as visitors. A whole young chicken stuffed with glutinous rice, ginseng and jujube arrives bubbling in a thick, nutty broth made with ground grains and seeds. The restaurant spreads through several connected hanok rooms, so big groups are seated quickly. It is a short walk from Gyeongbokgung Station — ideal after the palace.
tips: The line looks long but moves quickly — the hanok has many rooms.
Open 10:00–22:00 daily; go before 11:30 or after 14:00.

name: Okdongsik
summary: Michelin Bib clear pork gomtang at a tiny wooden counter in Hapjeong — Jirisan black pork, paper-thin slices, kimchi mandu.
description: Okdongsik reinvented dwaeji gukbap as a crystal-clear, gomtang-style broth made only from the legs of Jirisan black pigs. Rice is warmed by repeatedly pouring broth over it (toryeom), and thin slices of pork fan across the top. The room is a minimalist wooden counter with very few seats, so it suits small splits of the group rather than five together. It has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand since 2018 and is still listed in 2026.
tips: Counter-only and tiny — a family of five will be seated in pairs; go off-peak.

summary: The original Dongdaemun dakhanmari since 1978 — a whole chicken simmered at your table, then noodles in the broth.
description: Dakhanmari ('one whole chicken') was born in the alleys of Dongdaemun, and this three-storey restaurant claims the original recipe from 1978. A whole chicken arrives in a basin of broth with potatoes and rice cakes, simmering on a burner at your table; you dip pieces in a mix of chilli paste, soy, vinegar and mustard. Finish by adding kalguksu noodles to the rich broth. It is loud, fast, cheap and open until 1 am — perfect after Dongdaemun shopping.

tips: One chicken feeds about two to three; for five order two plus noodle sari.

summary: Gyodae's beloved 'second-floor house': flower-cut pork belly grilled for you, 12 minutes' walk from home.
description: Ijeung Jip ('the second-floor house') has been a Gyodae office-worker favourite for more than a decade, and the main branch is a short walk from home. name: Noryangjin Fisheries Wholesale Market
summary: Seoul's giant live-seafood market: pick crab, fish and shellfish from the tanks, then eat it sliced or steamed upstairs.
description: Noryangjin is Seoul's main wholesale seafood market, now housed in a modern multi-level building beside Noryangjin Station. The ground floor is a sea of glowing tanks – king crab, snow crab, flounder, abalone, scallops, sea squirt – with vendors calling out prices. You buy by weight downstairs, the vendor cleans and slices it, and you carry it up to one of the 2nd-floor 'sangcharim' restaurants, which charge a per-person table fee and extra for steaming or for a spicy fish stew (maeuntang) made from the leftover frames. It is loud, wet-floored and brilliantly theatrical; the upstairs rooms are plain and functional rather than pretty.
highlights: Steamed king crab or snow crab (daege), with crab-butter fried rice made in the shell
Hoe (sliced raw fish) platter – flounder (gwang-eo) and rockfish (ureok)
Maeuntang – spicy stew made from the fish frames
Live scallops, abalone and prawns grilled or steamed upstairs
tips: Prices change daily and are per kg – check the TPirates (인어교주해적단) app for the day's going rate, agree the weight and total before anyone starts cleaning, and don't be shy to compare two or three stalls.
Upstairs restaurants charge a table-setting fee per person (e.g. Chungnam Sikdang lists ₩5,000 pp; maeuntang ₩10,000–15,000) plus steaming fees – ask the fee before sitting down.
Floors are wet and fishy downstairs; wear closed shoes. The building has parking and elevators, and upstairs restaurants take groups of 5 easily.
From home: Line 9 express from Express Bus Terminal reaches Noryangjin in about 10 minutes; use Line 9 Exit 7 or Line 1 Exit 9 and follow signs.

name: Pro Soy Crab (Sinsa main branch)
summary: Seoul's best-known soy-marinated raw crab house since 1980 – roe-packed female blue crab, 3 min from Sinsa Station.
description: Pro Soy Crab has served ganjang gejang – raw female blue crab cured in soy – on the same Sinsa corner since 1980, and now fills a multi-storey building with around 300 seats. The crab arrives cold and glossy, the shell full of orange roe; you squeeze the sweet flesh onto rice, then mix rice into the shell with the soy and wrap it in laver. The spicy yangnyeom version is sticky, sweet and garlicky, and the crab-roe bibimbap is a gentler option for anyone wary of raw seafood. It is busy, efficient and very used to international guests.
highlights: Ganjang gejang – soy-marinated female blue crab (2 crabs per order)
tips: For 5 people, one large ganjang + one large yangnyeom order plus a roe bibimbap covers a tasting; rice is extra (a reviewer paid ₩1,000 a bowl) and refills are expected.
Prices are high and in-store menus may not match Naver's listing (one July 2026 reviewer paid ₩136,000 for the extra-large two-crab order) – ask the price for each size when ordering.
Locals say order the gyeran-jjim (steamed egg) and skip the crab stew; the soy crab is the reason to come.
Exit 4 of Sinsa Station, 150 m then into the Starbucks side street; valet parking ₩4,000. Group seating is available on several floors.
